After the first line `[\xff` from the same NUL-terminated witness buffer has already passed the section-header gate, the inner loop splits on the newline and returns the second line `$ncpus\xff`. That exact 7-byte option string is the attacker-controlled value later duplicated into the heap buffer that `fio_keyword_replace()` overreads.

`fio_options_parse()->dup_and_sub_options()` forwards the parsed option line into `fio_option_dup_subs()`. This helper only substitutes `${...}` environment references, so the plain reserved keyword survives unchanged and `strdup(out)` allocates the 8-byte heap buffer `$ncpus\xff\0` that AddressSanitizer later identifies as the overread region.

`fio_keyword_replace()` scans the duplicated option against the reserved-keyword table and the `$ncpus` entry matches at the start of the 8-byte buffer. The replacement loop therefore executes for this option instead of leaving the string untouched.

Inside the matching iteration, `o_org` saves the pre-advance `opt` value, aliasing the start of the 8-byte heap buffer. Later length arithmetic reuses this saved base pointer after `opt` itself moves to the suffix.
Because step 3 found the keyword at buffer offset 0, this subtraction derives `olen = 0`. There is no preserved prefix before the matched `$ncpus` token in the exact witness option.

Advancing by `strlen("$ncpus") + olen == 6` moves `opt` from the start of the 8-byte buffer to the one-byte tail `\xff` immediately before its terminating NUL. The saved alias from step 4 still points at the start of that same buffer.

After step 6 the remaining suffix length is exactly 1, so this guard is true and the suffix-copy path executes. The check proves only that some tail exists; it does not require the later `memcpy` length to fit inside the bytes remaining after the advanced `opt` pointer.
